Great insight — you clearly grasp why public access is risky. Now consider this: Class A declares Class B as a friend and gives B direct access to its private balance field. B can read and modify balance without any validation. Does this arrangement preserve data hiding, or does it create a hidden vulnerability? ```cpp
class A { private: int balance; friend class B; }; ```

I see you recognize that friendship breaks data hiding — that's a solid observation. But consider this: even when Class B 'needs' access, what if B accidentally passes balance to a third party? ```cpp
class A { private: int balance; friend class B; }; class B { public: void leak(A& a) { return a.balance; } }; ``` The need for access doesn't create a safety guarantee. So what protects balance if B itself is compromised?
